title: The Blood of Dawnwalker
description:
Bringing together a talented team of developers, including members of the core team behind one of the most acclaimed games of all time - The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt along with its expansions, Rebel Wolves’ first title is a dark fantasy narrative sandbox, AAA action-RPG set in medieval Europe.

This brand-new IP is aimed at mature audiences and is powered by Unreal Engine 5.

letsplay.title: I played 100 HOURS of The Blood of Dawnwalker — is it any good?

conclusion.summary: Блогер крайне положительно оценивает The Blood of Dawnwalker, называя её отличной игрой для тех, кто ценит сюжет и персонажей. Он особо выделяет проработанный мир, интересные квесты и систему боя, которая сочетает в себе экшен и стратегию. Основной особенностью игры является система ограничения времени (30 игровых дней), которая заставляет игрока планировать свои действия и выбирать приоритеты. Несмотря на наличие некоторых технических багов, блогер полностью рекомендует игру.

segments.text: So, I've played The Blood of Dawnwalker. A lot of it, actually. My first playthrough took me about 65 hours, and then I went back and did a whole lot more, which, well, I spent all of that time with the game, because The Blood of Dawnwalker is absolutely amazing, at least in the ways I care about most. It has its flaws, and one aspect of this game is going to be incredibly controversial, I am positive. In fact, I wasn't in love with it myself. But if you're someone who enjoys RPGs for their stories and their characters, then this game is a home run, and...

It's kind of insane that I'm saying that, because this game doesn't even have a main quest, and let me quickly explain how that works. So, as most of you know, in The Blood of Dawnwalker, you play as Coen, a half-human, half-vampire hybrid who needs to save his family. His siblings and parents are being held prisoner at a castle by an ancient and very powerful vampire named Brencis, who also happens to be the ruler of the valley this game takes place in. Vale Sangora, it's called. Brencis intends to kill Coen's family after 30 days of imprisonment,

which is a plan that Coen isn't exactly crazy about. That's the premise of the game. There's an opening prologue that establishes it, you know, it gives you a peek at Coen's family life to get you caring, and it also explains how everything went to hell in terms of the family being imprisoned and Coen's transformation into a half vampire because he starts out as a normal guy, but that's about all you get. The game then spits you out into its huge open world and says, have at it, do whatever you want. There's no main quest for you to follow, there's nothing at all you're required to do.

And in fact, if you want, you can just attack Brentsis immediately as a very underpowered individual, but you probably shouldn't do that because the entire world is at your disposal for 30 in-game days and nights that you can use to prepare. To attack and strategically take down Brentsis' allies, to find allies of your own through extensive and amazing story-heavy questlines, or to just focus on strengthening yourself through the many, many, many upgrades hidden throughout the game. Armor, weapons, ancient magic, secret permanent buffs for Koen,

There is so much to find, but the catch is that going after those things will cost you time. You have eight segments of time to spend each day and each night, and there's a meter at the top right of your screen to help you keep track of the hours and how many days remain before the family are set to die. Now, despite what you might have heard elsewhere, the truth is that virtually everything in The Blood of Dawnwalker has a time cost, and trying to hide that or downplay it...

is just pointless. Many Blood of Dawnwalker videos have claimed that only super important story things move time forward, and that you're free to explore the open world to your heart's content, but that is far from true. Now yes, if you want to be a little pedantic you can walk in a circle picking flowers infinitely, and that wouldn't progress time even a millisecond, but the moment you decide to complete something as simple as getting the treasure from a treasure map you acquired, or helping a person in danger during an open world event, or clearing a camp of enemy guards...

Those are all things that will cost you time in this game, and there is precious little that doesn't. A safe assumption is that if there's a point of interest on your map, it's going to cost you to clear it, unless it's a fast travel point, or one of the towers you can climb to reveal points of interest. Those are the two big exceptions, although even the fast travel points, some of them are broken and need to be restored, which, you guessed it, costs time. There's honestly just not much you can get away with in The Blood of Dawnwalker without time progression very quickly becoming a factor.

You can kill straggler enemies in the woods, you could, I guess, start certain quests and abandon them the second you see a time icon, because the game does do a good job of telling you exactly when time is gonna move, but ultimately, you are not meant to avoid spending time, because the reality is that you have plenty of it, and it's not meant to stress you out, even if it probably will occasionally. The devs told me a few months ago, when I went to a preview event for this game, that most of what you won't see in your first playthrough won't be because of time constraints.

It'll instead be alternate quest outcomes and different game endings and that sort of thing, and I found what they said to be completely true. By the time I hit the 30 day mark, I didn't have any story quests left to do, other than a glitched one, I guess. And the only things I had done to conserve time was choosing to not throw it away during a few situations where you could wait somewhere for day to become night or vice versa because some quests do require it to be a specific time of day. And I also had decided early on that I was not going to bother with every single treasure hunt.

and that I was gonna skip unimportant enemy camps. And by unimportant, what I mean is... Okay, quick interruption here for one last thing on the time system, because I probably should mention this. You might have heard that The Blood of Dawnwalker doesn't end after 30 days. That's something the developers have been saying for months, but that's only true if you're not interested in saving Coen's family. The game does give you a lot of freedom, so just not attacking Brentsis before the 30 days are up is something you can do, but...

Well, it probably isn't something most would want to do, for obvious reasons. Anyway, back to explaining what I meant by skipping unimportant camps. So, one of the coolest things about the open world content in Dawnwalker is that each region of the map belongs to a different Brencis ally. There's Ambris, a young vampire who was a total loser in his human life, which really shines through. There's Xanthe, a very ancient and mysterious figure. She's even older than Brencis. And then there's Bakir, who's a sort of jolly but at the same time very sadistic vampire.

who I found very entertaining. Now, the map in Dawnwalker is very loosely divided into their three territories. Brencis rules the valley, but his friends, his underlings really, have various operations across it. Operations that you can sabotage. For example, Ambris runs a huge blood harvesting network, where peasants are rounded up and drained by the very creatively named Blood Guards, and you can attack those bases and destroy what they've been storing.

Or you can target little camps where they've been forcing peasants to gather leeches they use as preservatives, or as another example, you can go directly after transports that are delivering the blood to Brencis. And anyway, doing that type of relatively simple content will not only increase your infamy, a system we'll talk about in a minute, but it will also anger whichever of the three Brencis underlings you're sabotaging at the moment. Anger that increases the more you get in their business, and once you've maxed out their anger meter, which is something you can keep track of in the menu,

You'll unlock a questline specific to dealing with each of them. To Ambrus, to Xanthe, to Bakir. These are long, story-heavy quests where you're making big choices. They are some of the best content in the game. But when I said unimportant camps earlier, when I talked about skipping them, what I meant is that once you've fully angered one of the underlings, there's really not much of a reason to continue attacking their bases. You can, but it'll cost you time, and it'll increase your infamy for no good reason, which really isn't something you want to do.

As your Infamy rises, there are nine levels, and it's another thing you can track in the menu, but as it rises, Brencis will issue Edicts, which are new rules for the valley that make your life harder. Prices will go up, eventually dramatically, roadside guard camps will appear that attack you on site and cost you time to engage with, eventually mercenary mini-bosses get sent out too, and the main gates to the big city Svartrou, those can even close permanently at a certain point, which can make getting in and out a nightmare. Infamy is not something you want to increase unnecessarily, although

I did it for the purposes of seeing how far it could go and I really did love how the game would occasionally let me use my high infamy as a way to scare off bandits and other enemies. Now to talk about the story a bit, if you're skeptical that a game like The Blood of Dawnwalker could have a great one, I really don't blame you.

I mean, how do you tell a compelling story when quests can be done in any order, and literally every quest other than the prologue can be skipped entirely? And the answer is really just that the setup of Coen needing to save his family is strong enough to propel you into the open world, and once you're out there, the game just delivers. It has the most interesting world, lore-wise, that I've explored since The Witcher 3. There's just this really strong foundation for interesting situations because Brancis' rule isn't loved by most of the people, and it's also a pretty new thing for them.

The long and short of it is that a couple years before the game's beginning, the plague had taken over the valley, killing thousands, and Brencis saw that as an opportunity to swoop in and take over, to kill the human leadership and anyone else who objected. So, fast forward a couple years, and many in the valley hate him. He forces everyone to give blood, his goons abduct innocent people and imprison them, and it's just a very dark time. However, not everyone hates Brencis. Life wasn't great before him, the previous human ruler wasn't exactly beloved,

Plus, the plague killed many, and one thing that vampires do for the humans of the valley is keep them healthy. They hold blood masses at the church, where the vampires drink from the humans, and the humans drink the blood of Brencis, because it has healing properties. Humans never get sick under his rule and are kept very healthy, which obviously benefits Brencis and the other vampires just as much as it does the humans. The word cattle comes to mind. Charming. That's one way to put it. Point is, though, it's a very interesting world that continually makes good on that great premise.

The big linear quest lines, which are mostly related to finding allies for yourself or dealing with Brencesses, those are the equivalent to main quest content in this game, and they're all excellent while having virtually nothing to do with each other. I mean, the Brencess ones sorta connect because all of his underlings know each other, so there are references between quests depending on what you've already done, but the paths that Coen can go down for allies, they just see Coen exploring very, very different parts of Vale Sangora.

For example, the rebellious underbelly versus digging into the vampire side of the world. They couldn't be more different, so they're very self-contained, with the only connective tissue being that Coen, in one way or another, is working towards his goal of defeating Brentsis. I don't want to spoil anything, so I won't, but this game just delivers. The smaller, side-quest-feeling questlines are just as good, and even the more filler-type open-world stuff, it all has the flair that good open-world games do. Little well-written conversations that flesh out what was happening,

in-game notes everywhere that often punch you in the gut. This is my kind of game, to put it very mildly, and it also helps that Coen is a character who is very easy to like. I really would describe him as being quite similar to Geralt, at least on the surface. He's a pretty level-headed guy who is a good person, and making decisions as Coen is very similar to The Witcher games because of it. He's not an evil dude, so you can't do many evil things in this game, although

There is this mechanic at night where, if Cohen is thirsty for blood, he can either accidentally, or through your input, give in to his hunger and kill the people he's talking to. This can be done to almost anyone, even important characters, which will end their questline, and in certain situations it can also be used to your advantage. I really don't want to say much, though, about the choices you make in this game. It's very much in spoiler territory, but...

You make quite a few of them and the game will hit you from time to time with very surprising follow-ups to past decisions. Let's end the story talk though and get into combat, which, well, The Blood of Dawnwalker has two very different combat systems. During the day you're just a human with a sword, albeit a human who also has access to some ancient blood magic you get very early on, and by night you're a savage vampire with a variety of absolutely brutal combat abilities, not to mention that you can also teleport and walk on walls and transform into a wolf.

And you might think, based on that description, that the daytime gameplay is less fun than the nighttime, but that is not the case at all because The Blood of Dawnwalker has some of the most fun melee magic combat I have ever played. Overall, the combat is a really nice mix of action and strategy. In a lot of ways, it is very straightforward witcher-esque action combat, but the biggest difference is that you control which direction you attack and block from, and you're greatly rewarded for being strategic with it.

Blocking in the direction an enemy is attacking from will let you block with no stamina loss, and a perfect block, so a well-timed one in the right direction, will open the enemy up and leave them super vulnerable. You can also just block without aiming, the game calls it an Omniblock, but it's a lot less efficient and it'll cost you stamina you don't want to be wasting. Attacking enemies is similar. You can do it without picking a direction, Cohen Swings will just be randomized in that case.

But by manually controlling your attacks, you'll land way more hits, as long as you don't swing in the same direction multiple times. Plus, pretty early on, there's also a skill you unlock that makes attacking in specific directions increase your damage, which you're going to want to take advantage of, because if I had one issue with the combat, it's just that enemies can really be health sponges at times, although Cohen's magic was a big help with that issue. Cohen accesses spells through runes that he carves into his skin, and because it's ancient blood magic you're tapping into, each spell you use will take away a bit of your health.

Although you can really build into that as you level up and make the health loss work in your favor or just counter it completely. The magic in Dawnwalker isn't super complex or anything. I don't want to oversell it. You're ultimately just using D-pad abilities on a cooldown. But for me, it was very satisfying sending swarms of ravens after enemies and boiling their blood from the inside. Magic also lets you do some non-combat things like slow down time so you can quickly run around. It lets you speak to dead NPCs and it gives you the ability to perform certain rituals throughout the game and

In total, there's like seven different spells in The Blood of Dawnwalker. It's not a ton for sure, but I found it to be enough because you're only using magic half the time anyway. Once nighttime rolls around, it goes away. Lore-wise, that's because Coen's skin heals very quickly as a vampire, so he can't keep the casting wounds open, but it doesn't really matter because everything you have access to during the day has a nighttime counterpart. For example, healing is done with food as a human, whereas at night, Coen has to drink blood to heal.

Spells are replaced with various vampire-specific abilities like exploding your enemies, and you can also put your sword away to use your claws instead, although I stuck with a sword for most of my playthrough. Swords can be used day and night, unlike the claws, and more importantly, upgrading your sword and claw damage both use a lot of the same resources, money and skill points, that you need for upgrading most things, so it was just more efficient, for me at least, to focus my resources on one weapon, the one I could use all the time.

Which, by the way, The Blood of Dawnwalker has three different skill trees, a magic-heavy one for Human Koen, another for his vampire form and related upgrades, and a third for more general things that benefit both, like health and stamina, and certain abilities like the one where you throw pocket sand, which can be used both day and night. Like I mentioned, all three trees use the same pool of skill points, which you get from leveling up and doing certain activities, plus most upgrades have a time cost as well. You start with only basic upgrades available to invest in, but...

Then as you play, you'll unlock more. Vampiric abilities unlock the more you drink blood throughout the game. Every time you drink, your corruption will rise and each level of corruption comes with newly available skills. And for other abilities, you just need to find or buy skill books out in the world. That's how you unlock new alchemy recipes too. There's a limited crafting system in the game where you can make various healing items and stamina boosts and similar. And to get new recipes, you just find them or buy them.

To wrap this review up though, and by the way if you've enjoyed it I'd really appreciate it if you could leave a like, it really helps get my videos out there, and as I'm recording this I am currently pulling an all-nighter trying to get this video done in time, but let's talk about bugs and performance, which I wish I could say I had no issues here, but not quite. If you're worried about the game being a buggy mess it definitely isn't, but I did have a couple of NPCs get stuck which made me reload certain quests, the main city did have a recurring issue where the ground would just flicker in and out of existence from time to time,

and I had a quest that was inaccessible. Anytime I approached it, I'd just start losing health and die, which I can't begin to explain. I also had a recurring problem where it would switch from day to night or vice versa, and Cohen would just randomly have no pants on. I couldn't figure that one out. I checked to make sure I had pants equipped for both day and night a million times because you can have different day and night equipment presets, but despite having pants equipped for both, they'd just disappear from time to time. Other than what I mentioned though, essentially no other bugs. Most sessions I'd go hours without a single issue.

Performance was mostly fine as well, 4K easily clearing 60fps with ultra settings on a 4090, although I did have some limited crashing problems, for some reason always at the main menu, which seems pretty fixable if it's a widespread issue. I think that about wraps this review up though. I loved The Blood of Dawnwalker and recommend it wholeheartedly. It's full of great characters, amazing quests, really fun combat, and it looks pretty damn nice too.
